catalog_quote: In Kristang most polysyllablic words fall into two large classes according to the position of stress in the word. These classes follow two stress rules: Stress Rule A. Most words which end in a vowel are stressed on the penultimate syllable, as in kaza (= ka + za) 'house' ... kumeria (= ku + me + ri + a) 'food' ... Stress Rule B. Most words ending in a consonant are stressed on the final syllable, as in landes (= lan + des) 'Dutch', natal (= na + tal) 'Christmas'. Nevertheless, stress is not completely predictable in Kristang as there are certain words which are exceptions to the above two rules. Exceptions to rule A (i) One large class of exceptions to rule A above consists of verbs which end in a stressed vowel. new_statements.quote: Papiá Kristang is a syllable-timed language. The two largest stress groups are words with tonic stress on the penultimate syllable, as in kaza ‘house’, and on the final syllable, as in kumí ‘eat’. Smaller stress groups are those words with a stressed antepenultimate syllable, such as kólera ‘cholera’, and some monosyllables such as kí ‘what?’. [...] Tonic stress is indicated on vowels and syllabic nasals by a written accent when the tonic does not fall on a penultimate syllable or to differentiate stressed and unstressed monosyllabic words.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Malacca Creole Portuguese (src qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so this chapter supplies the first placement statement: a penultimate/final lexical split with antepenultimate and monosyllabic residue. Nothing to contradict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically fixed per word and not derivable from syllable count or weight: the two largest classes are penultimate-stressed words (kaza 'house') and final-stressed words (kumí 'eat'); smaller classes have antepenultimate stress (kólera 'cholera') or are stressed monosyllables (kí 'what?'). Penultimate is the orthographic default (unmarked); non-penultimate stress is written with an acute accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate-stressed words (kólera) and stressed vs unstressed monosyllables are the minority classes; no weight or morphological conditioning is stated in this chapter (the word-class split, verbs final vs non-verbs penult, is given in Pillai, Baxter & Soh 2019, not here).
new_statements.identity_note: Papiá Kristang is the self-name of Malacca Creole Portuguese (mala1533), spoken in Malacca, Malaysia; Baxter's chapter examples are informant-elicited in Malacca (2010). The JIPA 2019 illustration calls the same language Malacca Portuguese Creole (MPC) and is based on one speaker from the Portuguese Settlement, Malacca. No other variety is described.

sources.quote: 'MPC differs from Malay as it has lexical stress' (p.93). 'the stressed syllable is longer and has a higher intensity compared to the unstressed ones ... In general, MPC has a large number of words displaying penultimate syllable stress, as in kaza [ˈka.zə] house, floris [ˈflo.ris] flower. This is especially the case in words ending in a vowel, provided they are not verbs. A second large class of words, principally verbs, take final-syllable stress, for example, kumí [ku.ˈmi] ... However, even in cases where we may predict word-final stress ... the speaker sometimes stresses the first syllable
sources.note: Only IPA Illustration / quasi-instrumental statement on Kristang stress; confirms the V-final-penult / C-final-final / verbs-final picture and documents verb-stress variability in running speech; worth adding to refs as the modern corroborating source.
